title: Global Payments Report 2026: How Payments Companies Can Regain Investor Confidence
gist: Payments stocks have de-rated sharply (25% below 10-year average valuation, -6% TSR over four years vs +20% for the S&P 500) as volume growth matures and AI investor capital rotates elsewhere; BCG argues AI will widen rather than close the gap between share-taking leaders and laggards, and that business-model exposure to this reset varies enormously across acquirers, vertical SaaS, issuers, networks, and new segments like BNPL and digital assets.

insights.claim: Payments companies now trade roughly 25% below their 10-year average valuations and nearly 50% below their prior peak, with total shareholder return of -6% over the past four years versus +20% for the S&P 500 overall.
insights.speaker: Albane de Vauplane
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of the de-rating; investors should treat payments as a sector-wide repricing event, not isolated single-name weakness.
insights.quote: many payments companies now trade at roughly 25% below their 10-year average valuations and nearly 50% below their prior peak
insights.locator: After decades of strong growth, many payments companies

insights.claim: The payments de-rating is driven by three converging forces: volume growth slowing as digital payments penetration and cash-to-card conversion mature, intensifying competition that separates a small group of share takers from a much larger group of share donors, and investor capital rotating into the AI trade and away from payments.
insights.speaker: Albane de Vauplane
insights.so_what: Explains the mechanism behind the multiple compression, useful for distinguishing cyclical from structural drivers when re-underwriting payments names.
insights.locator: The shift reflects more than a change in investor sentiment

insights.claim: Investors are no longer rewarding raw transaction-volume growth; they now pay up for revenue backed by deeper customer engagement and higher switching costs, built through multi-product attachment, network effects, or end-to-end transaction optimization.
insights.speaker: Albane de Vauplane
insights.so_what: Investors should screen payments holdings for stickiness (attach rate, switching costs) rather than headline volume growth, since volume-only growth is being actively discounted.
insights.quote: Volume growth alone is no longer enough.
insights.locator: Volume growth alone is no longer enough

themes.theme: AI as a moat-widener, not a leveler

insights.claim: Contrary to investor fears that AI will commoditize payments capabilities, BCG's research suggests AI instead widens existing competitive gaps because already-strong performers use it to cut costs and improve products faster, raising the cost of falling behind for slower-moving competitors.
insights.speaker: Albane de Vauplane
insights.so_what: Argues for staying long the category leaders through an AI cycle rather than rotating into laggards on hopes of AI-driven catch-up or commoditization.
insights.quote: Our research, however, suggests that AI could instead widen existing competitive differences.
insights.locator: AI is also directly reshaping payments itself

insights.claim: For leading vertical SaaS payments platforms, AI is more likely to reinforce than erode their edge, because their distribution, workflow integration, industry expertise, and financial-services capabilities are hard to replicate, and AI lets them add functionality quickly and capture more value from commerce already flowing through their platforms.
insights.speaker: Albane de Vauplane
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the market narrative that AI threatens vertical software differentiation, a potential contrarian long thesis for premium-multiple vertical SaaS payments names.
insights.locator: Vertical SaaS commands a premium, but the advent of AI

insights.claim: As AI agents take on a larger role in the purchasing journey, competition to be the 'top of wallet' payment method will begin earlier in the transaction flow, requiring greater investment in discovery, personalization, authorization, and fraud prevention -- a bar that may be difficult for smaller issuers to clear while reinforcing the advantage of the strongest players.
insights.speaker: Albane de Vauplane
insights.so_what: Flags agentic commerce as a coming share-shift catalyst in card issuing; watch for consolidation pressure on sub-scale issuers as agent-mediated purchasing grows.
insights.quote: the competition to be “top of wallet” will begin earlier

insights.claim: Across the payments sector, operating expenses rose 9% annually over the past three years versus revenue growth of only 7%, and as growth slows from high-single-digit to mid-single-digit rates, this stubbornly high cost base threatens to push margins into reverse.
insights.speaker: Albane de Vauplane
insights.so_what: A concrete operating-leverage red flag: investors should model margin compression risk for payments companies that haven't yet rationalized cost structures, especially those with fragmented tech and dispersed operations.
insights.quote: Operating expenses have risen by 9% annually over the past three years, compared with revenue growth of 7%.
insights.locator: Costs are growing faster than revenue

insights.claim: Top vertical SaaS-based payments acquirers trade at roughly 2.8 times the valuation multiple of traditional acquirers and processors, a premium supported by category dominance, deep payments embedding in customer operations, and a unified technology backbone that limits technical debt.
insights.speaker: Albane de Vauplane
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete multiple benchmark for the vertical-SaaS-versus-traditional-processor valuation gap when relative-value trading the payments space.
insights.quote: The top vertical SaaS-based acquirers trade at roughly 2.8 times the valuation multiple of traditional acquirers and processors.

insights.claim: Traditional acquirers and processors are the most exposed business model because merchants and orchestration platforms are increasingly routing transactions by price, authorization rates, and service level, pushing legacy providers behind third-party software where they lose the direct client relationship and the pricing power that underpins their valuation.
insights.speaker: Albane de Vauplane
insights.so_what: Identifies substitution/disintermediation as the key downside risk for legacy acquirer/processor stocks -- a screening factor for avoiding value traps in the group.
insights.locator: Acquirers and traditional processors are most at risk

insights.claim: Card issuing remains highly profitable with leaders taking share, but tailwinds are fading as cash-to-card conversion matures and account-to-account payment schemes expand, while regulatory headwinds intensify in markets such as Brazil and Australia and loom in the form of possible EU interchange caps and lower US debit interchange rates.
insights.speaker: Albane de Vauplane
insights.so_what: Issuer economics face a multi-front regulatory and structural squeeze; investors should track interchange rulemaking in the EU and US as a near-term catalyst for issuer margins.
insights.locator: Issuing is a rich business for sophisticated players

insights.claim: Card networks retain formidable core franchises and strong valuations that give them substantial M&A capacity and scaling ability, but investors are questioning how defensible their newer bets in core banking, digital assets, and cybersecurity are relative to their core payments business.
insights.speaker: Albane de Vauplane
insights.so_what: Networks' capital firepower supports continued bolt-on M&A, but investors should distinguish core-franchise value from optionality on unproven adjacencies when underwriting network valuations.
insights.locator: Networks need to prove that they can grow beyond the core

insights.claim: BNPL and digital assets are new, scaled payments segments attracting significant investor interest for their profitable-growth potential, but both remain early-stage and it is still unclear which players will become large, enduring franchises.
insights.speaker: Albane de Vauplane
insights.so_what: Frames BNPL and digital-asset payments plays as high-optionality, unproven bets rather than established compounders -- size positions accordingly.
insights.locator: New payments segments show promise, but are unproven

insights.claim: BCG lays out a three-front playbook for payments executives to regain investor confidence: simplify and focus capital on segments where durable differentiation is achievable, invest in long-term durability (SaaS players expanding geography/features without losing focus, traditional acquirers adding subscription/leasing/financing revenue, issuers pursuing B2B and connected commerce, networks building a neutral trust layer via tokenization), and align the investor base with whether the company is a growth story or a value story.
insights.speaker: Albane de Vauplane
insights.so_what: Gives investors a checklist to score payments management teams against: portfolio simplification, revenue-durability investments, and honest growth-vs-value investor guidance -- companies failing on these fronts are likely to keep de-rating.
insights.locator: Regaining Investor Confidence Requires Hard Choices

insights.claim: Companies facing structurally slower growth must proactively decide whether to conduct a formal investor reset -- resetting guidance and repositioning as a value story -- rather than continuing to be judged against a fading blue-chip growth narrative.
insights.speaker: Albane de Vauplane
insights.so_what: Signals that more payments companies may pre-announce guidance cuts or strategic repositioning; investors should watch for explicit growth-to-value repositioning announcements as a sector catalyst.
insights.quote: companies facing slower growth must decide whether they should conduct an investor reset
insights.locator: Align your investor base with the business
